author: reek
body: A base is a signed, compressed copy of a range of the log's own sectors.

author: reek
body: The artifact is SMALLER than what it holds. That assertion is the whole point of stating it out loud: four chapters in a since-deleted compression quire compressed nothing, and every one of their tests passed, because a pass-through round-trips perfectly. A round-trip test cannot tell a compressor from a pipe. This one can.

author: reek
body: The three refusals. An untrusted signer is refused. A tampered artifact is refused, and refused BEFORE it is expanded -- the artifact hash is checked on the bytes as handed over, which is the only order that can decline a decompression bomb. And what comes out is checked against the plain hash the same signature covered, so a decoder that is subtly wrong cannot pass itself off as history.

author: reek
body: And the round-trip: the bytes that come back out are the log's sectors, byte for byte, which is what makes the artifact a fact log rather than a thing shaped like one.

author: reek
body: THE .disk SIDECAR IS LOAD-BEARING. Without a disk attached, every write is dropped and every read returns zeros -- and this test PASSED that way while it was being written. It reported a real compression ratio (3072 zero bytes compress wonderfully) and an exact round-trip (zeros round-trip perfectly), because the archive machinery agreed with itself about nothing at all. Only the last assertion, which needs a fact to actually be on the disk to read back, caught it. Delete the sidecar and this test goes green against an empty disk.
